## The Museum of Almosts

The museum occupied a narrow shop between a locksmith and a bakery that, for reasons never explained, sold only rye bread on Mondays.

Its sign read:

**THE MUSEUM OF ALMOSTS**  
**Admission: one hesitation**

The man found it on a Thursday afternoon, standing in the rain with a suitcase and an unused bus ticket.

He had missed the 3:40 bus to the coast. Not by much. He had watched it pull away while his daughter waved from the upstairs window, calling something he pretended not to hear. The next bus was not until five.

Inside, the museum smelled of dust, warm electrical cables, and old paper. A brass clock on the wall read 4:12, though its hands had no numbers.

“Help you?” A woman emerged from a doorway, wearing a gray cardigan and an name badge that said **ILSE — CURATOR**.

“I’d like,” he said, “to see the life I would have had.”

Ilse looked at his suitcase, then at the ticket in his hand.

“Most people do,” she said. “They’re usually disappointed.”

She led him past glass cases filled with ordinary objects. A coffee cup with two lipstick marks. An unopened letter addressed in his own handwriting. A pair of shoes placed neatly beneath a windowsill, as though their owner had merely stepped away.

“Do you have anything about today?” he asked.

“Today?”

“The life I would have had if I’d caught the bus.”

Ilse stopped before a large case at the end of the room.

Inside was a miniature coach, its windows glowing against a painted seaside. A tiny man with his face looked out from the glass. Beyond him stretched a white beach, a row of blue houses, and a sky the color of late apricots.

The man leaned closer.

The life inside the case was peaceful. A woman was playing guitar on a porch. Someone was chopping wood. A child ran after a dog along the water. It looked warm, clean, and generously lit—the sort of life that appears in advertisements for lives other people are having.

“Is that what would have happened?”

“No,” said Ilse.

He turned toward her.

“That’s what you imagine would have happened if you’d been braver.”

He stared at the little beach, the little guitar, the little version of himself who had apparently never hesitated.

“So where is it?”

“The almost is earlier.”

She pressed a concealed switch. The scene vanished. In its place was the back seat of the 3:40 bus, viewed from behind.

He saw himself looking out the window. He saw the ticket in his hand. He saw the moment he had looked at the old address written in the margin and realized, for the first time, that leaving might not be an adventure. It might be a failure wearing a beautiful coat.

A label beneath the case read:

**THE MOMENT BEFORE EVERY DEPARTURE  
WHEN DEPARTURE BECOMES REAL**

The museum was quiet except for rain ticking against the windows.

“I thought it was supposed to show me another future,” he said.

“Futures are easy to invent. Mostly we fill them in with whatever we wish had happened.” Ilse rested both hands on the edge of the case. “But before that, there is usually only a second. A breath. A choice made so quietly that you don’t notice until afterward.”

He looked at the miniature bus.

Inside it, his smaller self was still looking at the address.

“Can I have it?”

“Take the almost,” Ilse said. “The rest is only speculation.”

Outside, the rain had softened. The bakery lights glowed gold across the street. Somewhere up above his window, his daughter was probably still there, waiting for him to explain why he had let the bus go.

He sat down on the museum’s worn wooden bench. He placed the suitcase between his feet and the ticket on his knee.

For the first time in months, he did not picture the coast.

He pictured the next twenty minutes: the apology he would offer, the explanation he did not yet have, the evening that would be uncomfortable and unfinished and entirely his own.

At 4:27, Ilse began dimming the lights.

“The five o’clock bus comes at five-twelve,” she said.

“Then I suppose I have time.”

The suitcase was not going anywhere. The ticket was not going anywhere. And for once, neither was he.
